asks: A labelled diagram of a right-angled triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 units, showing a square drawn outward on each side, each square divided into unit squares, and the right-angle mark.
A drawing of a large square with four equal right-angled triangles placed inside it, showing the tilted square left empty in the middle and the four triangles labelled with their two shorter sides.
A standard diagram of a right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at B, showing the side AB, the side BC, the longest side AC and the right-angle mark.
picture.why: The squares on the three sides turn a rule about lengths into areas a learner can count: 9 small squares and 16 small squares fill the square of 25.

big_idea.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square drawn on the longest side has exactly the same area as the squares on the two shorter sides put together.

objectives.can: Work out the longest side of a right triangle from its two shorter sides
Explain why the squares on the two shorter sides fill the square on the longest side
Decide whether the rule can be used for a given triangle

why_it_matters.text: With it you can find a length you cannot measure, like how long a ladder must be to reach a window, from two lengths you can.

the_why.text: Four copies of the triangle fit inside one big square in two ways: once leaving the square on the longest side empty, once leaving the two smaller squares empty, so those empty spaces must have the same area.

picture.text: A right triangle with short sides 3 and 4 units and the right-angle mark; a square grows outward on each side, cut into unit squares (9, 16 and 25). Then the 16 tiles and the 9 tiles slide into the square on the longest side and fill it with none left over. Last, four copies of the triangle are arranged in a big square two ways to show why it always works.
picture.standard: squares drawn on the three sides of a right triangle

card.diagram_ask: A labelled diagram of a right-angled triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 units, showing a square drawn outward on each side, each square divided into unit squares, and the right-angle mark.

needs_first.text: The area of a square is its side times its side.
What a right angle is and how it is marked.

mistakes.mistake: Adding the two shorter sides to get the longest one: 3 + 4 = 7.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Going straight across is shorter than going along two sides; it is the areas of the squares that add, not the lengths.

mistakes.mistake: Using a² + b² = c² for any triangle.
mistakes.why_it_fails: It is true only when the angle between the two shorter sides is a right angle; in a triangle with sides 4, 5 and 6, 16 + 25 = 41 is not 36.

mistakes.mistake: Stopping at 25 (or 100) and giving that as the side.
mistakes.why_it_fails: 25 is the area of the square on the longest side; the side is the number that multiplied by itself gives 25, which is 5.

mistakes.mistake: Calling any side c, the side opposite the right angle.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Only the longest side, the one opposite the right angle, has the square equal to the other two together.

opening_question.question: A right-angled triangle has its two shorter sides 3 cm and 4 cm long. Without measuring, how long is the third side?

route.what: Show the right triangle with sides 3 cm and 4 cm and ask how long the longest side is. Ask for a guess.
Measure the longest side with a ruler on the screen: it is 5 cm, not 7 cm. So adding the sides does not work.
Grow a square on each side and count the unit squares: 9, 16 and 25. Ask: what do you notice about 9, 16 and 25?
Slide the 16 tiles and the 9 tiles into the big square: they fill it exactly. Then place four copies of the triangle in one big square two ways, so the empty spaces must be equal.
Name the longest side the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle, and write the rule as side × side for each square: a² + b² = c².
Open the right angle wider so it is no longer 90°: the longest side grows and the two small squares no longer fill the big one. The rule needs the right angle.
Work out the longest side when the short sides are 6 cm and 8 cm: 36 + 64 = 100, and 10 × 10 = 100, so it is 10 cm.
Short sides 5 cm and 12 cm: the learner finds the longest side (13 cm) before it is shown.
The learner says why the two small squares fill the big one, in their own words.

questions.question: A right triangle has shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the longest side?
questions.explain: 36 + 64 = 100 is the area of the square on the longest side, and the side whose square is 100 is 10 cm.

questions.question: A triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm has no right angle. Does 4 × 4 + 5 × 5 equal 6 × 6?
options: No: 16 + 25 = 41, not 36, because there is no right angle
Yes, it works for every triangle
questions.explain: The squares on the shorter sides fill the square on the longest side only when the angle between them is a right angle.

questions.question: A right triangle has sides 5, 12 and 13 cm. Which side is opposite the right angle?
options: 12 cm, any side can be the one
questions.explain: The side opposite the right angle is always the longest, so it is 13 cm, and 25 + 144 = 169.

try_it.title: Fill the big square
try_it.stands_for: Each small square of the paper is one square centimetre of area; the squares you cut stand for the squares on the triangle's sides.
try_it.predict: Will the 9 small squares and the 16 small squares together cover the square on the longest side exactly, with none left over?
steps: Draw a right triangle with shorter sides 3 cm and 4 cm on squared paper and measure its longest side with the ruler.
Cut out a 3 by 3 square and a 4 by 4 square from the squared paper.
Cut out a square whose side is the longest side you measured.
Lay the 4 by 4 square in one corner of the big square.
Cut the 3 by 3 square into its small squares and use them to fill the gap.
try_it.observe: The longest side measures 5 cm, and the 16 and 9 small squares cover the 5 by 5 square exactly, with no gap and nothing left over.
try_it.question: Why do the two smaller squares fill the big one exactly, when 3 + 4 is not 5?
try_it.expected: Because what adds up is the area of the squares, not the length of the sides: 9 + 16 = 25 = 5 × 5, and this happens because the triangle has a right angle.
try_it.write: In a right triangle the square on the longest side equals the squares on the other two sides together. 3 × 3 + 4 × 4 = 5 × 5.
try_it.in_class: Pairs: one draws and measures, one cuts. The teacher draws the 3-4-5 triangle with its three squares on the board and writes 9 + 16 = ?. Ask: did your small squares cover the big one, and why not 7? A pair whose squares do not fit has usually not drawn a true right angle.
